title: Zhaozhou's tea
hookLine: to every visitor, new or old: go and have some tea
tomorrow: The true person of no rank

cards: Two monks arrive at a monastery in northern China to see the Chan teacher everyone is talking about. He asks the first one, have you been here before? No, says the monk.
Have some tea, says the teacher. He asks the second one the same question. Yes, I've been here before.
Have some tea. The temple's manager has been standing nearby, and he can't stand it. Why, he asks, does the one who's new get tea, and the one who's been here get tea too?
The teacher calls his name. The manager answers, yes? Have some tea.

teach.h: THE SAME ANSWER FOR NEW AND OLD.
teach.b: First, the answer that doesn't change. A newcomer and a regular get the same reply. You might expect a teacher's answer to fit the question; here, Zhaozhou seems to throw the question away.
New or old, the cup is the same, and what counts is drinking it.
Second, the manager. He is the one who keeps track, who knows who has been here and who hasn't, and he wants the rule explained. Zhaozhou doesn't explain.
He calls him by name, and when the man answers, he gets tea too. The one asking for an explanation is offered the same thing as everyone else. Third, the phrase.
In Chinese it is three characters, chi cha qu. Readers differ on the last one.

teach.h: CHI CHA QU: GO, HAVE SOME TEA.
teach.b: Some hear it as go: go and have some tea, off you go. Others hear it as a softer ending: have some tea, then. Either way, it is the plainest thing a host can say, and Zhaozhou says it to everyone.
Fourth, why it lasts. Nothing in the story is mysterious.

teach.h: A CUP POURED, A CUP DRUNK.
teach.b: A cup is poured. Someone drinks it. Whatever you thought you needed to understand first can wait until the tea is gone.

how: Zen communities may serve tea as part of the day, and the story of Zhaozhou's tea is told in Zen teaching and calligraphy as a reminder to meet the present moment plainly.

o: the same plain cup a teacher offered every visitor
a rare tea served only to the most senior monks
a tea ceremony with strict steps for each guest

s: Zhaozhou gave the new monk and the returning monk different answers
both got the same reply: have some tea.
the manager who asked why also got tea
Zhaozhou called his name and offered him the same cup.
readers agree on exactly how to read the last character, qu
some hear go, some hear a softer ending; the reply is plain either way.

games.q: you're Zhaozhou. your manager asks why the new monk and the old one got the same answer. what do you say?
o: call his name, then offer him tea
games.why: Zhaozhou called the manager's name, and when he answered, said: have some tea.

practice: If there's a drink near you, tea, coffee, water, hold it in both hands; if not, remember the last cup you held, and feel its warmth or its cool against your palms.
Smell it, take one sip and let it rest on your tongue before you swallow, and when the mind reaches for the next thing, come back to the cup.

wordCard.voice: Zhaozhou's tea. The Chan teacher who gave every visitor, new or returning, the same reply: have some tea. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese chi cha qu: have some tea, or go and have some tea. Zhaozhou's reply to new and old alike.

carryVoice: Your line: have some tea. New or old, the cup is the same. That's day nine hundred eighty-eight.
